title: Generics
description: Learn how to write flexible, type-safe, reusable code with C# generics.

data.text: Generics allow you to write classes, methods, and interfaces that work with any type while preserving full compile-time type safety. Instead of boxing value types into object or casting back from object, generics let the compiler enforce the correct type from the start.

Before generics were introduced in C# 2.0, developers used the non-generic System.Collections namespace. An ArrayList could store any object, which meant the compiler could not help you catch mistakes. Worse, value types like int and double were boxed into object on every add and unboxed on every read — adding both type-safety risks and significant performance overhead.

data.title: Non-generic ArrayList — the old way
data.content: Demonstrates boxing and the risk of runtime cast errors

data.title: No More Casting
data.text: With generics, the compiler guarantees type correctness at compile time. A List<int> only accepts int — no boxing, no casting, no surprises at runtime.

A generic method declares its type parameters on the method itself, between angle brackets. The caller specifies the actual type when invoking the method, or the compiler can infer it from the arguments passed.

data.title: Generic Method — returning the default of any type
data.content: Shows explicit type specification and compiler inference

data.text: A generic class declares its type parameter at the class level, making the entire class type-safe for whatever type T is supplied. The most common real-world example is the generic Repository<T> pattern used in data access layers.

data.title: Generic Repository Pattern
data.content: A reusable data store that works with any entity type

data.text: Generic interfaces let you define contracts that work with any type. The built-in IEnumerable<T> is the most important generic interface in C# — it enables foreach iteration and powers LINQ. Defining your own generic interface lets multiple types share the same contract.

data.title: Generic Interface — IRepository<T>
data.content: Shows an interface contract consumed by multiple implementations

data.text: By default, a type parameter T can be replaced with any type. The where keyword lets you restrict T to types that meet certain criteria, such as being a class, a struct, having a parameterless constructor, or implementing a specific interface. Constraints unlock methods that would otherwise be unavailable on an unknown type.

rows: T must be a reference type
Can check for null, use reference-type equality
T must be a value (non-nullable) type
Guarantees no null; can use default without nullability warning
T must have a public parameterless constructor
Can write new T() inside the generic class/method
Can use BaseClass methods and properties on T
Can call CompareTo on instances of T

data.title: Multiple Constraints Applied
data.content: Demonstrates class + new() + interface constraints together

data.text: C# supports variance on interface and delegate type parameters using the out (covariant) and in (contravariant) keywords. Covariance allows a more derived type to be used where a base type is expected (output positions). Contravariance allows a less derived type (base) to be used where a more derived type is expected (input positions).

data.title: Covariance with IEnumerable<out T>
data.content: Assigning a derived-type sequence to a base-type sequence variable

data.title: Real-World Generics in .NET
data.text: Generics are everywhere in .NET: List<T>, Dictionary<TKey, TValue>, Task<T>, IEnumerable<T>, IQueryable<T>, Nullable<T>, and your own Repository<T> pattern all rely on them.

data.title: Exercise: Build a Generic Pair<T>
data.description: Create a reusable generic class that stores two values of the same type and a method to swap them.
steps: Define a class Pair<T> with two fields: First and Second.
Write a constructor that accepts two T values.
Add a method Swap() that exchanges First and Second using a temporary variable.
Write a method BothEqual() that returns true if both values are equal (use EqualityComparer<T>.Default.Equals).
Test your Pair<T> with int, string, and a custom class.
data.expectedOutcome: A fully functional generic Pair<T> class that demonstrates type parameter usage, EqualityComparer<T>.Default, and ref-swap logic.

items.question: Can generics have more than one type parameter?
items.answer: Yes — Dictionary<TKey, TValue> is the most common example with two parameters. You can have as many as needed: Tuple<T1, T2, T3, T4, T5, T6, T7, TRest>.

items.question: Are generics slower than non-generic code?
items.answer: No — the JIT compiler generates a specialized native version for each type argument at runtime. Value types avoid boxing entirely, so generics are often significantly faster than non-generic alternatives.

items.question: What is the difference between where T : class and where T : class?
items.answer: where T : class means T must be a reference type (string, classes, interfaces). In a nullable-enabled context, it also means T may be null. Use where T : notnull for types that must never be null.

items.question: Can I create a generic static class?
items.answer: Yes — a static generic class creates a separate static field instance for each closed type. This is useful for per-type caches or counters: static class Counter<T> { public static int Count; }

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Generics provide compile-time type safety without boxing
Constraints (where T :) restrict which types can be used
Common constraints: class, struct, new(), base class, interface
Generics power List<T>, Dictionary<TKey, TValue>, Task<T>, and LINQ
Variance (out/in) allows safe subtype assignment in interface types
Generic interfaces enable flexible, testable code
data.takeaway: Generics are the foundation of type-safe, reusable code in C#. Once you master them, you will see them everywhere in the .NET ecosystem.
